newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary NBH says lower inflation top 1997 priority.
newsitem.headline: Hungary NBH says lower inflation top 1997 priority.

text.p: The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) said on Thursday its monetary policy in 1997 would continue to focus on reducing inflation.
"The main objective remains the reduction of inflation," NBH President Gyorgy Suranyi told a news conference.

He expected year-on-year inflation to drop to 17 percent by December 1997 from an estimated 20 percent at the end of this month, and average annual inflation down to 18 percent in 1997 from about 23 percent in 1996.
The NBH would continue its cautious interest rate policies next year, keeping rates at levels which encouraged forint savings by promising sufficient real yields on deposits.
"Our policy has been to cut our repo rates from month to month or from week to week if necessary, following the decrease of inflation," he said.
Suranyi said one-year government paper currently offered up to 21.8 percent yields, offering sufficient real interest when compared with the 1997 December year-on-year inflation target.
The best-rated debtors in Hungary currently pay three to four percent real interest to creditors and this rate is likely to remain unchanged in 1997, he said.
But the government planned to improve the opportunities of small and medium-size enterprises, which have access only to loans with 26 percent or higher rates of interest, Suranyi said.

Suranyi said Hungary would continue its monthly 1.2 percent crawling peg devaluations in 1997, but the devaluation rate may be cut if inflation declined as planned and foreign trade processes were favourable in 1997.

The central bank president said he expected the pace of economic growth to pick up to two to three percent next year if exports increased by eight to 10 percent and wages maintained their real value, as planned.
Gross domestic product is expected to grow by up to one percent this year.

Suranyi said he hoped that increasing investment would contribute to the GDP. He said he doubted that figures showing a drop in investment volume this year were realistic as he believed private sector investment was dynamic.

"Machinery imports rose by 12 to 13 percent this year and this leaves serious doubt in me whether investments really declined," he said, adding that Hungary needed more imports aimed at investment even if it meant increasing its current account deficit.
